overview: This file traces Japanese marine shipbuilding from Depression-era consolidation proposals through increasingly secretive and centralized wartime control. It begins with 1930 plans to amalgamate shipbuilders, documents the industry's poor financial condition in 1932 and the restriction of commercial shipyard information by 1936, and reports a 1939 struggle among major shipping and shipbuilding companies over Kawasaki shares. Its centerpiece is an embassy analysis and full translation of the 1939 Shipbuilding Industry Law, which licensed firms, authorized subsidies and domestic-content requirements, regulated prices and specifications, organized compulsory trade associations, and imposed penalties. The final records concern shipbuilding finance and naval intelligence alleging construction of three or four Japanese battleships at Kure, Nagasaki, Yokosuka, or Kobe.

subfiles.title: Neville report on proposed control and amalgamation of shipbuilding
subfiles.doc_type: document-file note with attached telegram extract
subfiles.about: Reports official approval of proposals to amalgamate Japanese shipbuilders and establish a joint-management company.
subfiles.summary: The file note and attached extract record a late-July meeting of the Industrial Commission chaired by the Premier. The commission approved a committee plan to amalgamate shipbuilders, establish a company for joint management, and recommend the proposals to the government.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Neville on the financial condition of Japanese shipyards
subfiles.about: Provides financial figures showing losses and a poor outlook for Japanese shipbuilding companies.
subfiles.summary: Neville reports Japan's shipyards mostly unprofitable in 1930-31, with heavy losses and little new construction planned.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Donovan despatch on withheld shipyard statistics
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch explaining why monthly reports could no longer include construction tonnage for Kobe–Osaka shipyards.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Kobe-Osaka shipyards stopped sharing tonnage-under-construction figures with the consulate.

subfiles.title: Scott despatch on suppression of Japanese shipbuilding information
subfiles.from: Winthrop R. Scott, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports the disappearance of detailed construction-stage statistics from a Japanese shipping journal, probably under military-police pressure.
subfiles.summary: Scott reports a Japanese shipping journal quietly dropped detailed construction data in 1936, suspecting military-police pressure and broader censorship.

subfiles.title: Gourley report on Osaka Shosen’s purchase of Kawasaki shares
subfiles.from: N. K. Gourley, American Consulate, Kobe
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Investigates the contested purchase of 400,000 Kawasaki Shipbuilding preferred shares by Osaka Shosen Kaisha.
subfiles.summary: Gourley reports Osaka Shosen bought Kawasaki shares pledged to a bank, via Yamashita Steamship, prompting Kawasaki's demand for their return amid shipping-industry consolidation.

subfiles.about: Describes the escalating rivalry over 400,000 Kawasaki Shipbuilding preference shares and efforts to mediate the dispute.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: Kawasaki Steamship opposes the transfer of its shares to Osaka Shosen, seeking mediation between the firms.

subfiles.title: Dooman despatch analyzing the Shipbuilding Industry Law
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits and explains the Japanese Shipbuilding Industry Law promulgated in April 1939.
subfiles.summary: Dooman summarizes the law’s licensing, subsidy, domestic-content, financing, price-control, technical-standard, and reporting provisions. He connects the legislation to shipping demands created by the war in China, the diversion of merchant vessels from normal routes, and comparatively high Japanese construction costs. The despatch interprets the law as part of a broader movement toward the regimentation and socialization of Japanese industry. It also anticipates further government control of the shipping industry itself.

subfiles.title: Embassy translation of Law No. 70, the Shipbuilding Industry Law
subfiles.from: Japanese Government; translated by the American Embassy at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Provides the complete English translation of Japan’s 53-article Shipbuilding Industry Law and its supplementary provisions.
subfiles.summary: The law restricts shipbuilding licenses to qualifying Japanese-controlled companies and subjects business transfers, suspensions, mergers, dissolution, financing, equipment, production, prices, technical standards, and research to government direction. It authorizes subsidies, compulsory use of Japanese products, propulsion tests, land expropriation, extraordinary debenture issues, and compensation for certain ordered losses. Articles 17–41 establish and closely regulate Shipbuilders’ Associations and their federations, including compulsory membership or compliance when ordered. The final articles extend supervision to related manufacturing and repair, prescribe fines and imprisonment for violations and bribery, and provide transitional arrangements for existing businesses.

subfiles.title: Naval attaché report on Japan’s battleship building program

subfiles.summary: Kelly reports a source's claim that Japan was building three or four battleships at named shipyards.
